diasporas

/dye-AS-per-uhz/ - the stress falls on AS · noun

What It Means

Diasporas are populations that have spread far from their ancestral homeland.

The port city's food festival grew out of its three great diasporas, each cooking the dishes of a homeland most of the cooks had never seen.

Example

A linguist mapping the world's Greek and Gujarati diasporas found the same pattern in both: the scattered communities kept wedding songs alive long after the villages they came from had let the tunes go.

Diasporas is more exact than immigrants or emigrations because it names the scattered peoples themselves — whole communities, generations deep, still tied to a homeland — not the individuals or the act of leaving.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

dispersions: A dispersion is the scattering itself, or the scattered state — of seeds, particles, or people. Diasporas are always peoples: whole communities living far from an ancestral homeland, generations deep and still tied to it. A dispersion can be over in an afternoon; a diaspora persists and remembers.

exiles: Exiles are individuals forced out of their country, often one by one and against their will. Diasporas are collective and can be voluntary: entire scattered communities that keep a homeland's identity alive for generations. One banished poet is an exile; his descendants' communities abroad may become a diaspora.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

natives: the people still rooted in the ancestral land

returnees: those who have made the journey back home

Where it sits · how large and lasting the migration — tourists → settlers → diasporas

tourists vs. diasporas: Tourists are the lightest case, nowhere near a diaspora — away from home for weeks with return tickets in their pockets, they plant no community abroad and leave nothing lasting behind.

settlers vs. diasporas: Settlers stay for good, but one family putting down roots abroad is not yet a diaspora — that word waits for a whole people, scattered and persisting for generations.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — dia-

Prefix — dia-: across, through

Root — spora

Root — spora: a sowing, a seed (Greek speirein, to scatter)

Suffix — -s

Suffix — -s: plural: more than one

Put it together

Put it together: Dia- (across, through) + spora (a sowing, a seed — from Greek speirein, to scatter) + -s (plural) = seeds scattered across the world. The image is agricultural: a people cast like seed over distant ground, taking root wherever they land. Biology keeps the root in spore, the drifting seed of ferns and fungi.

Use the root in a new word: spore

Use the root in a new word: spore: A single puffball can release a trillion spores into one gust of wind.

Root Check

Word Choice

academic / journalistic

Diaspora — and its plural, diasporas — is the scholar's and journalist's word for scattered peoples themselves, not for the journey they made. Use it for communities generations deep; for an individual newly forced abroad, exile (a word in this unit's reference list) or refugee is more exact. And mind the number: one diaspora is one scattered people.
